column2: This is the order that matters. Write the lead to storage, then attempt the email, the CRM push, the WhatsApp alert and the conversion event. Every one of those can fail without losing the enquiry. Reverse the order and a single failure loses a customer silently.
A sane setup, in order
<t0>Make the lead durable first</t0>Ensure form submissions are stored somewhere that is not an inbox. Everything downstream is optional; this is not.
<t0>Turn on call assets with a forwarding number</t0>This captures the people who ring straight from the ad without ever visiting your site, usually a bigger share than owners expect.
<t0>Add website call tracking with number swapping</t0>So calls made after landing on the site are attributed too. Test it on a real phone, because the swap depends on a script running.
<t0>Set a minimum call duration</t0>Sixty seconds is a reasonable default. Adjust once you have listened to a sample of real calls.
<t0>Import the conversion and let it settle</t0>Do not judge the change for at least two weeks. Bidding algorithms need time, and a fortnight of local-service call data is a small sample.
Where this advice stops

Call recording is a separate decision from call tracking, with separate legal obligations that vary by country and sometimes by region. Knowing that a call happened, how long it lasted and which keyword produced it is enough to optimise campaigns. Recording its contents is a bigger step, take advice before you do it.

And my sample here is two businesses, in two countries, in two industries. The mechanics generalise; the numbers do not. I have not published a cost-per-call figure in this article because I do not have one I can stand behind for a named account with a stated date range, and a made-up benchmark would be worth less to you than this sentence.
Do you know which searches produce your phone calls?
Most local businesses running Google Ads cannot answer that. Send me your site and I will tell you what is being tracked and what is not.

Google Ads Conversion Tracking Not Working: Diagnostic Order
Google Ads showing no conversions has a short list of causes. Here they are in diagnostic order, with a check for each and why a working tag can report nothing.

Google Ads reporting no conversions has a short list of causes, and they are not equally likely. Here they are in diagnostic order, with the check for each, plus the reason a working tag can still report nothing for weeks.
Google Ads conversion tracking
Why is my Google Ads conversion tracking not working?

The most frequent causes are the tag not being present on the page that confirms the action, the conversion action being set to a category or count setting that hides it, the tag firing but not being linked to the right conversion action, consent settings blocking the tag, and attribution windows meaning the conversion has not been reported yet.
How long does Google Ads take to show conversions?

Conversions can take up to 24 hours to appear in reporting, and conversions are credited to the date of the click rather than the date of the conversion. That means recent days always look worse than they eventually will, which is a normal reporting artefact rather than a fault.
How do I test if my Google Ads conversion tag is firing?

Use Google Tag Assistant in debug mode, complete the conversion action yourself, and confirm the conversion tag fires with the correct conversion ID and label. Then check the conversion action status in Google Ads, which should move from Unverified to Recording conversions.
Google Ads says zero conversions. You know you got the sale.

Google Ads reporting zero conversions usually comes down to one of five things: the <t0>tag is not on the page that confirms the action</t0>, the tag fires but is not linked to the right conversion action, the conversion action is excluded from the “Conversions” column, consent settings are blocking it, or the conversions exist but have not been reported yet because they are credited to the click date.
The last one is not a fault, and it fools people constantly.

This is one of the most-searched tracking problems there is, and the search results are dominated by forum threads where nobody arrived at an answer. That tells you something: the symptom is generic, and the cause is usually specific to how one account was wired.
So rather than listing every possibility, here is the order I actually work through, which resolves most cases in the first three steps.
Before you change anything: is it actually broken?

Google Ads credits a conversion to <t0>the date of the click</t0>, not the date the conversion happened. Someone who clicked on Monday and bought on Thursday appears in Monday’s row, and until Thursday, Monday looks worse than it really was.

The practical effect is that <t0>recent days always understate performance</t0>, and they keep filling in for as long as your conversion window allows. If you are looking at the last three days and concluding tracking is broken, you may just be looking at data that has not finished arriving.
<t0>The test that settles it</t0>

Look at a period that ended at least two weeks ago and is fully outside your conversion window. If that period has conversions and recent days do not, your tracking works and you were reading an incomplete report. If that older period is also zero, keep reading.
The diagnostic order
The conversion action status tells you where you are
Google Ads → <t0>Goals</t0> → <t1>Conversions</t1> → <t2>Summary</t2>. Each conversion action has a status, and it is the fastest diagnostic in the whole account.
<t0>No recent conversions</t0>: the tag was seen once but nothing lately. Usually a page or template changed.
<t0>Unverified</t0>: Google has never received a signal. The tag is not firing where you think it is.
<t0>Inactive</t0>: nothing for a long period. Treat as broken.
<t0>Recording conversions</t0>: the tag is fine and your problem is elsewhere, most likely the next item.
<t0>The check</t0>Read the status before touching any code. It tells you whether this is a tagging problem or a reporting problem, and those have completely different fixes.
The conversion is recording but excluded from the column

This one produces the maddening version of the problem: the conversion action clearly shows conversions, but your campaign view says zero. The cause is the <t0>“Include in Conversions”</t0> setting. If it is off, that action still records, it just does not appear in the Conversions column, and Smart Bidding does not bid toward it.
Secondary conversion actions are deliberately excluded by design. If someone set your main purchase action as secondary, everything looks broken while working perfectly.
<t0>The check</t0>Open the conversion action and confirm the primary/secondary setting matches what you want to optimise toward.
The tag fires but carries the wrong label

A Google Ads conversion tag needs both a conversion ID and a conversion <t0>label</t0>. The ID identifies the account; the label identifies which action. Copy a tag between two conversion actions and forget to change the label, and the tag fires perfectly, into the wrong bucket.
<t0>The check</t0>In Tag Assistant, complete the action and read the conversion label on the fired tag. Compare it character for character with the label in the conversion action’s tag setup.
Consent Mode is denying storage, and you have not modelled for it

If you added a consent banner (and in the UK and EU you should have), tags now wait for permission. That is correct behaviour. But a banner configured to default everything to denied, with no consent update wiring, means the conversion tag never gets its permission and never fires.
This one has a signature: conversions drop off a cliff on the exact day the banner went live.
<t0>The check</t0>Load the site fresh, accept cookies, complete the action, and confirm the tag fires. Then repeat and reject, and confirm it does not. Both directions must behave as intended.
The tag is not on the page that actually confirms the action

The classic. The tag is on the site but not on the thank-you page, the order-status page, or the page a customer reaches after a payment provider redirects them back. On lead-gen sites, the equivalent is a form that submits by AJAX without a page load, so a page-view-triggered tag never gets a chance to fire.
<t0>The check</t0>Perform the conversion yourself, then view source on the page you land on and search for the conversion ID.
Once it works, make it measure money
Getting the tag firing is where most people stop. It is the point at which the interesting work starts, because a conversion count treats every lead as identical, and yours are not.

For lead-gen accounts, <t0>enhanced conversions for leads</t0> plus offline conversion imports let you send the real value of a closed job back to Google Ads. Bidding then optimises toward revenue instead of form-fills. That is the difference between an algorithm chasing enquiries and one chasing customers.

The mechanics are the same as the call-tracking work in <t0>the local service post</t0>, capture the click identifier at submission, store it with the lead, and send the value back when the job is won.
Limits

The order above is a search order, not a frequency table, it reflects a small number of accounts and the logic of each failure mode, not a study. Google Ads changes its interface regularly, so I have anchored the checks to statuses and tag payloads rather than menu locations wherever I could.

What is a click ID?
A unique identifier that Google Ads adds to your landing page address when someone clicks an ad. Storing it with the lead lets you tell Google Ads later which click produced which job.
Do I need to build a plugin?
No. The requirement is to store each lead with its click ID and report the outcome back to Google Ads. I wrote a plugin because this client's form was also losing leads when emails failed.
Why not just track form submissions?
A form submission shows interest. A booked job shows revenue. If only the first is reported, Google Ads has no way to learn which clicks lead to the second.
Telling Google Ads which leads became booked jobs
Google Ads can only optimise toward the outcomes it is told about. If your tracking stops at the form submission, bidding learns to find people who fill in forms.
Sending the click ID and the real job value back to Google Ads lets it optimise toward revenue instead.
This is the approach I used for a UK carpet cleaning business in Slough. I am describing the method here, and the project is still ongoing.
The problem it solved
The site launched on a standard Elementor form, which is email-first: it composes an email and sends it. If that send fails, there is no second copy. The lead is gone and nobody knows it existed.
On top of that, Google Ads had no way of seeing which clicks turned into booked jobs, so it was optimising toward form submissions.
How the fix works
<t0>Save the lead first</t0>Every lead is written to a database table before any email, webhook or API call is attempted. A failing third-party service can then never break lead capture.

<t0>Capture the click ID and campaign parameters</t0>At submission, the Google click ID (gclid) and UTM parameters are stored with the lead, so each lead stays linked to the ad click that produced it.
<t0>Record the outcome</t0>Pipeline stage, job value and notes are logged against each lead, so the question of what the ad spend earned can be answered from the data.
<t0>Send the value back</t0>The real job value is pushed back to Google Ads as an offline conversion, including enhanced conversions for leads, so bidding can optimise toward booked jobs.
What I built, and what you actually need

I built the whole thing as a self-owned WordPress plugin called LeadBridge, with no paid dependencies and no third-party middleman holding the data. I did that because this client needed the form fixed as well.
You do not need my plugin to use the method. You need the four steps: store every lead safely, keep the click ID with it, log the outcome, and report the value back to Google Ads.

As Google describes it, enhanced conversions for leads adds hashed customer data, such as an email address, to the click ID so that a match can still be made when a click ID is missing. That is why the lead record should hold both.

How many pages does a local service business need?
One for each service you want to be found for, with the areas you cover described on it. Add separate area pages only when you have something genuinely different to say about each area.
Is a Google Business Profile enough on its own?
It is a strong start for Maps and local search, and it works better alongside a website with a page for each service. I treat them as parts of one setup.
It depends on local competition and the starting state of the site and profile, so I do not quote a fixed timeline.
<t0>Field Notes</t0>  /  Local SEO
One page per service and area: how I structure local SEO for a service business
For a local service business I build a dedicated page for each service and the areas it covers, instead of one page trying to rank for everything.
On a UK carpet cleaning site I created separate pages for carpet, sofa, mattress and commercial cleaning, aimed at Slough, Berkshire and the surrounding areas.
A business that offers four services usually has one page that mentions all four. That page gives both the visitor and Google a weak match for each individual search.
Why separate pages

Someone searching for sofa cleaning wants a page about sofa cleaning. A page about carpets, sofas, mattresses and commercial work serves none of those searches well. A dedicated page lets each search land on exactly what the person asked for.
What each page needs
One service and one clear heading
The page title and main heading name the service and the area, so the page is obviously about one thing.
Content that belongs to that service
What is included, what the job involves and which areas you cover for it. Content that only makes sense for this service.
Trust signals next to the claim
Reviews, certifications and before and after photos placed on the page, where a visitor decides whether to call.
The fixes around the pages

The pages work better when the basics around them are right. On the same project I corrected page titles, meta descriptions, heading structure, image alt text and internal links, set up and optimised the Google Business Profile, and verified Search Console and worked through the crawl and indexing issues it showed.
<t0>The trap to avoid</t0>

Do not clone one page and swap the town name. Google's spam policies call pages created to rank for specific, similar search queries, such as place variations, doorway abuse. Each area you name should have something genuinely specific to say.

Taking over a Meta account means inheriting undocumented decisions. Audit measurement before creative, because every judgement rests on unverified numbers.
Auditing an inherited Meta account
What should I check first when auditing a Meta ad account?

Check the measurement layer before the campaigns. Count the pixels installed, reconcile reported purchases against real orders for a settled week, and confirm which pixel each campaign optimises toward. Judgements about creative and targeting are only as good as the conversion data underneath them.
How long does a Meta ads audit take?

The measurement checks take a few hours. The reconciliation needs a settled week of data that is at least two weeks old so attribution windows have closed. Rebuilding after a fix needs a further day or two of clean data before performance can be judged.
What does it mean if inherited campaigns show high ROAS but low revenue?

It usually means the conversion data is inflated. Common causes are duplicate pixels, purchase events firing on pages that are not orders, or duplicate events between the browser pixel and the Conversions API. Reconcile reported purchases against actual store orders before trusting any campaign-level number.

The first thing to audit in an inherited ad account is not the ads.
<t0>Kamran Arshad</t0><t1>13 Aug 2026</t1><t2>9 min read</t2>

When you inherit a Meta account, audit the <t0>measurement layer before the campaigns</t0>. Count the pixels, reconcile reported purchases against real orders for a settled week, and map which pixel each campaign optimises toward.
Every judgement you are about to make, pause this, scale that, rests on conversion data you have not yet verified. Verify it first.

Most audit checklists start with creative, audiences and structure. Those matter. They matter <t0>second</t0>, because each one is judged against reported performance, and reported performance is exactly the thing an inherited account gives you no reason to trust.

I took over an account where doing this in the wrong order would have been expensive. The best-performing campaigns in Ads Manager were producing nothing. Audit the creative first and you would conclude those campaigns had the winning angle, and put more money behind them.
<t0>Where these figures come from</t0>

One Shopify account I took over and audited, a skincare brand running Meta ads at roughly <t0>PKR 100,000 per day</t0>. The client asked me not to name them, so I have not. The numbers are as they stood in the account during that engagement.

This is <t0>one account</t0>, not a study. I am giving you the mechanism and one worked example, not an industry statistic. And I am not stating precise engagement dates here because I would rather omit them than approximate them.
Phase one: can these numbers be believed?

<t0>Count the pixels</t0>Shopify: <t1>Settings → Customer events</t1>, the <t2>Facebook & Instagram sales channel</t2>, and <t3>theme.liquid</t3> searched for <t4>fbq</t4>. Then confirm in the browser with DevTools, because configured and firing are different things. More than one pixel ID is a finding, not a detail.

<t0>Reconcile a settled week</t0>Events Manager purchases versus real store orders, same week, same timezone, at least two weeks old. Events Manager should approach your order count and never exceed it.

<t0>Map campaigns to pixels</t0>For every active campaign, record which pixel its conversion event is configured against. This is the step that turns a vague discrepancy into a specific list of campaigns.

<t0>Trace each group’s orders</t0>Take the campaigns attached to each pixel and try to find their claimed orders in the store. A group whose orders cannot be traced is your problem, and you now know exactly how much budget it holds.
<t0>Check the Conversions API setup</t0>If CAPI is running, confirm deduplication is actually working rather than merely configured, see <t1>the deduplication article</t1>.
<t0>The question that ends phase one</t0>

Can you state, in one sentence, how many purchases the store made last week and how many Meta thinks it made, and explain the gap? If not, do not touch a budget yet. Every optimisation you make is a bet on numbers you cannot defend.
